clue.text: Warranty timed from point of delivery

indicators.note: the answer is made from these letters, worked into a new order, so 'from' signals rearrangement here

explanation.surface: A guarantee's clock starts running at the moment goods are handed over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivery' looks commercial, as does 'Warranty', but the delivery is of a baby. 'from' is a thin anagram signal: the thirteen letters of WARRANTY TIMED are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Babies are delivered in a hospital ward set aside for childbirth, so that ward is where delivery happens.

clue.text: Noah, a master of spin

definitions.meaning: Noah built the ark, and a builder or maker is a wright
Sir Richard ... invented the water-powered spinning frame in 18th-century England

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spin' suggests a spin doctor, but it is cotton spinning.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the cotton-spinning inventor also describes Noah's trade of ark-building, since a wright is a maker.

clue.text: Last salmon in the lake could get you a prize

indicators.note: the final letter of salmon goes inside the name of the lake

parts.note: Lake Erie, one of the North American Great Lakes

indicators.note: only the final letter of the word salmon is used, as 'Last' says

explanation.surface: The last fish an angler lands from the lake might win a competition.
explanation.walkthrough: ERNIE is the machine that picks the winning numbers for UK Premium Bonds, a state savings scheme paying prizes instead of interest.
explanation.definitionFit: The Premium Bond number-picking machine is what selects prizewinners, so it is what could win you money.

clue.text: Where lines meet lines between poles

indicators.note: the poem's letters sit between the two pole letters

parts.note: the North and South poles, abbreviated N and S
an ode is a poem, that is, lines of verse

explanation.surface: Telegraph lines strung between poles meet at junctions.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'lines' are lines in a graph or network; the second are lines of poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: In a network or graph, junction points where several connecting lines come together are called this.

clue.text: S is very hush-hush

parts.note: the letter S is what you get as the top (first letter) of the word secret

explanation.surface: Someone whispers that a single letter is classified information.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer, read as wordplay, means 'the top of secret', which is the letter S.
explanation.definitionFit: Classified at the highest level, a document marked this way is extremely confidential.

clue.text: Tuesday about one I set off, which is most easy to manage

indicators.note: the actress's surname goes round the numeral

parts.note: Tuesday Weld is an American film actress
the Roman numeral for one is I

indicators.note: set off suggests the letters of I SET are knocked out of order

parts.note: taken as written for the anagram

explanation.surface: Someone sets off on a Tuesday, looking for whatever will be simplest to handle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tuesday' looks like a day of the week, but it is the first name of the American actress Tuesday Weld, whose surname is the piece wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A tool that is easiest to handle is the most manageable one to brandish or control.

clue.text: Breed little sunbeams, as they say

indicators.note: signals that the word is heard rather than read, a sound-alike

parts.note: rays are narrow beams of sunlight

explanation.surface: Bright little rays of sunshine help things grow, people say.
explanation.walkthrough: Breed here is a verb, to rear animals or children.
explanation.definitionFit: To rear livestock or bring up children is to breed them.

clue.text: Worldwide conflict — a way no good for the big problem

parts.note: global means worldwide
war is armed conflict
the M1 is a British motorway, a road written as MI with an I for the numeral one

explanation.surface: A worldwide war, a road that is no use, all adding up to one huge issue.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the motorway from London to Leeds; crosswords write its 1 as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Climate change from rising temperatures is often called the greatest challenge facing the planet.

clue.text: Chats of little significance

definitions.meaning: chats are a variety of small new potatoes, a British term
the phrase is an idiom for things that are unimportant

explanation.walkthrough: 'Chats' looks like conversations; it means small potatoes grown for eating whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally tiny tubers, the phrase idiomatically describes anything trivial or unimportant.

clue.text: Compared to having given wrong information about Livingstone

indicators.note: the verb for lying goes round the first name

parts.note: to have lied is to have given false information
Ken Livingstone was Mayor of London

explanation.surface: Someone is accused of misreporting facts about the explorer Livingstone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Livingstone' suggests the explorer David; it is Ken Livingstone, the London politician and first elected Mayor of London.
explanation.definitionFit: To say one thing resembles another is to compare them; the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Dutchman with misplaced pursuit of devotion?

parts.note: Piet is a common Dutch first name
an ism is a doctrine or cult followed with zeal, often said dismissively

explanation.surface: A Dutch man devotes himself to a pursuit that seems wrong-headed.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is loose: an emphasis on religious feeling is a form of devotion.
explanation.definitionFit: Extreme religious piety, stressing personal devoutness, is a kind of devotion.

clue.text: Whig said to be a fool

indicators.note: signals a sound-alike: the word is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: berk is British slang for a fool

explanation.surface: A member of the Whig party is mocked as an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: Edmund Burke was an 18th-century Whig politician and writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Edmund Burke sat in Parliament for the Whigs, the liberal party of 18th-century Britain.

clue.text: Veronica is OK after drug use

indicators.note: the word for being OK comes after the drug

parts.note: speed is slang for amphetamine
to be well is to be OK, in good health

explanation.surface: Veronica is fine after taking drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Veronica' looks like a woman's name; it is the botanical genus of the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Veronica is the botanical name for this small blue-flowered plant genus.

clue.text: Help for student, say, in college

parts.note: L, the plate shown by a learner driver
e.g. is short for 'for example', which 'say' can mean
up means in residence at university

explanation.surface: Someone helps a student who is at college.
explanation.walkthrough: A UK learner driver displays an L plate, so a student is L.
explanation.definitionFit: A boost given to someone to help them climb or progress is a helping hand.

clue.text: Ray Hooper unfortunately gets it in the mouth

indicators.note: signals that the name's letters come out in a bad, disordered way

explanation.surface: Poor Ray Hooper gets hit in the mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets' is the link: the answer is the 'it' that he gets in his mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Gum disease with discharge of pus is an affliction found in the mouth.

clue.text: Lash for a hack party official

parts.note: a hack is a horse for ordinary riding
a whip enforces party discipline in Parliament

explanation.surface: A party disciplinarian lashes out at a hack journalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hack' looks like a journalist; it is a riding horse.
explanation.definitionFit: To lash someone is to beat them with a whip such as the kind used on horses.

clue.text: Ill with the hay fever — hardly living thus

indicators.note: fever suggests the letters of ILL THE HAY are thrown into turmoil

explanation.surface: A hay fever sufferer is hardly living in good health.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is a link and 'hay fever' is split: 'fever' is the anagram signal. The definition is ironic: someone ill with hay fever is hardly living in good health.
explanation.definitionFit: Being well is the opposite of having hay fever, so a sufferer is hardly living this way.

clue.text: Theatre — or second-hand book fair?

definitions.meaning: the Theatre Royal ... is a London theatre
Hay-on-Wye is a Welsh town full of second-hand bookshops, a market for books

explanation.walkthrough: Hay-on-Wye is a Welsh border town famous for its many second-hand bookshops and literary festival.
explanation.definitionFit: A London theatre bears this name, which can also be read as a market at the Welsh book town.

clue.text: A 23 across nutcracker for Yuri

annotationWithheld.why: A 23 across nutcracker for Yuri (9) for ASTRONAUT: A + anagram of ROAST + NUT, but 'nutcracker' is one word giving both the fodder NUT and the anagram indicator 'cracker', a word doing two jobs

clue.text: Assignation in racetracks

annotationWithheld.why: Assignation in racetracks (5) for TRYST: the parse needs TT (race) around RYS (tracks, railways), so the single word 'racetracks' gives two pieces, and no sound parse was found

clue.text: Gathers matter, USA style

indicators.note: the letters are arranged in a different fashion

explanation.surface: Something collects material in an American way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'matter' is fodder here, but it also hints at the meaning: to gather pus, which is called matter.
explanation.definitionFit: A boil that gathers forms pus, which is what to maturate means in medicine.

clue.text: Judge in Germany

definitions.meaning: one who tries a case is a judge
An ancient city in western Germany

explanation.walkthrough: Trier is a city on the Moselle in Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: One who tries a court case is literally a trier, and a German city bears the same name.

clue.text: Instrument turns up free, though not at first

indicators.note: in a down clue, the remaining letters are read upwards
the opening letter of the word for free is dropped

parts.note: gratis means free of charge

explanation.surface: An instrument appears for nothing, though not straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping G from GRATIS leaves RATIS, which 'turns up' reads backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The sitar is a long-necked plucked stringed instrument from India.

clue.text: Cook, as in trash

indicators.note: the word as sits inside the word for rubbish

parts.note: rot means rubbish or nonsense

explanation.surface: A cook is in the bin.
explanation.definitionFit: To roast is a way of cooking meat in an oven.

clue.text: Hot iron used to identify an animal

indicators.note: used suggests the letters are worked over into a new arrangement

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A hot iron is used to brand an animal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests branding cattle; 'to identify' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhinoceros is a large thick-skinned African or Asian animal.

clue.text: Take note about an African capital losing head and one another

indicators.note: the note letters go round the beheaded city

parts.note: NB, nota bene, means take note

indicators.note: the city name drops its first letter

parts.note: Cairo is the capital of Egypt
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone notes that an African capital has lost its leader and one more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing head' drops the C from Cairo. 'another' is the definition, read as another African capital: the setter leans on 'African capital' earlier in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital of Kenya is another African capital besides the one in the wordplay.

clue.text: Bamboozle the European drip

parts.note: to trick is to bamboozle or deceive
le is the French word for 'the'

explanation.surface: A European is tricked by a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drip' looks like a wet person; here it is a thin flow of liquid.
explanation.definitionFit: A drip of liquid, flowing slowly, is a thin trickle.

clue.text: Margaret madly involved with lad by the sea

indicators.note: madly signals that the letters are jumbled

parts.note: a youth is a lad

explanation.surface: Margaret is crazily involved with a young man.
explanation.walkthrough: Great Yarmouth is a seaside resort in Norfolk, England. The anagram uses YOUTH, a synonym of 'lad'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norfolk resort lies on the North Sea coast, so it is a town by the sea.
